topic.title: Respiratory surfaces and the effect of exercise on breathing
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: Two reliable slots. The adaptations come as a ruled-line matching item worth [4] (Summer 2025 B1 F Q3, where only better candidates linked them all). The exercise half is a graph question of 6 to 9 marks — March 2026 B1 F Q7 asked for the start of exercise, its duration, a range, a completed recovery line and evidence that one student was fitter, and the unit overview named it the most challenging question on the paper.
mustMemorise: Respiratory surface: large surface area, thin, moist, permeable, good blood supply, diffusion gradient maintained
Thin = short diffusion distance; moist = gases dissolve; blood supply = the gradient is maintained
Oxygen diffuses alveolus → blood; carbon dioxide diffuses blood → alveolus
Exercise increases BOTH the rate and the depth of breathing
notOnThisSpec: The mechanism of ventilation: ribs, intercostal muscles, diaphragm and pressure changes are not a learning outcome in §1.5
Lung volumes, tidal volume and spirometer traces
Oxygen debt as a named process (1.5.5 asks only for a comparison of aerobic and anaerobic respiration)
The structure of the airway beyond the alveolus

note.title: Respiratory surfaces and the effect of exercise on breathing
note.subject: science

mustKnow: The six adaptations: large surface area, thin, moist, permeable, good blood supply, diffusion gradient maintained
Exercise increases both the rate and the depth of breathing

notOnThisSpec: The mechanism of ventilation (ribs, diaphragm, pressure)
Oxygen debt as a named process

mustBeAbleTo: List the six adaptations of a respiratory surface
Match each adaptation to what it does, in one ruled line each
Give the direction each gas diffuses at an alveolus, and why
Explain how a good blood supply maintains the diffusion gradient
Apply the same six ideas to a leaf or to an unfamiliar animal
State that exercise increases both the rate and the depth of breathing, and explain why
Read a resting rate, a peak rate and a duration off a breathing graph
Complete a recovery line so that it levels out at the resting rate, not at zero
Give evidence for a conclusion by quoting a value for each of the two things compared
Calculate a percentage increase using the resting value as the denominator
sheet.howExamined: B1 is 1 hour: 60 marks at Foundation, 70 at Higher, calculator allowed. Respiratory surfaces appear as a matching item of [4] — one ruled line from each adaptation, with more explanations printed than adaptations. The exercise half is a graph question of 6 to 9 marks built from [1] readings, a [1]-[2] line to complete and a [2]-[3] evidence part. Schemes are point-for-point, the listing rule applies to every ruled line and every one-word answer, and an evidence mark needs both things compared and a number for each.
traps: Listing the adaptations without saying what each one does — the reason carries the mark (Summer 2025 B1 F Q3)
Swapping 'thin' and 'large surface area' in the matching item
Giving the blood supply without the words 'maintains the diffusion gradient'
Reversing the oxygen and carbon dioxide gradients (Summer 2023 B1 F Q2(b))
Saying only that breathing gets faster, and leaving out depth
Reading the end time of exercise as its duration (March 2026 B1 F Q7(a)(ii))
Reading from the wrong line when two students are plotted
Drawing the recovery line down to zero instead of levelling it at the resting rate (March 2026 B1 F Q7(a)(iv))
Giving evidence with no numbers in it (March 2026 B1 F unit overview)
Dividing by the peak instead of the resting rate in a percentage increase

workedExamples.stem:
The graph shows two students' breathing rates before, during and after exercise.
(a) Use the graph to give the resting breathing rate of student X. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage increase in student X's breathing rate from rest to its highest value. Show your working out. [3]
(c) Give two pieces of evidence from the graph that student Y is fitter than student X. [2]

steps.working: resting rate of X = 16 breaths per minute
steps.decision: Read the flat part before the exercise starts, not the first point after it. A resting rate is a flat line, which is why the graph gives you ten minutes of it.

Because the peak is the larger number
Because the graph starts at zero
whyMenu.explain: Percentage increase = change ÷ original × 100, and the original here is the resting rate.

steps.working: Y rests at 12 breaths per minute and X at 16; Y peaks at 28 and X at 36.
steps.decision: Two pieces of evidence, each with two numbers. A comparison needs both students named, and CCEA's schemes say so explicitly.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: (a) 16 breaths per minute. (b) 125%. (c) Y has the lower resting rate (12 against 16) and the lower highest rate during exercise (28 against 36).

twin.stem: Student Y's breathing rate rose from 12 at rest to 28 breaths per minute. Calculate the percentage increase. Give your answer to one decimal place.

items.stem: Which adaptation explains why gases dissolve before they diffuse across a respiratory surface?
items.skill: Match an adaptation to its explanation

options.feedback: Gases have to dissolve in the film of liquid before they can diffuse through the wall.
Thin gives a short diffusion distance. That speeds diffusion up, but it is not what lets the gases dissolve.

options.text: It has a large surface area
options.feedback: Surface area means more room for diffusion at once. Dissolving needs liquid.

options.text: It has a good blood supply
options.feedback: The blood supply carries gases away and keeps the diffusion gradient going.

items.stem: Oxygen diffuses from an alveolus into the blood. Which way does carbon dioxide diffuse?
items.skill: Get the direction of each diffusion gradient right

options.text: From the blood into the alveolus
options.feedback: Blood arriving at the lungs is high in carbon dioxide and low in oxygen, so each gas moves the opposite way to the other.

options.text: From the alveolus into the blood
options.feedback: That is the direction oxygen goes. Summer 2023 examiners reported candidates getting the oxygen and carbon dioxide gradients the wrong way round on exactly this item.

options.text: Carbon dioxide does not diffuse at the alveolus
options.feedback: Both gases cross at the alveolus; that is what gas exchange means.

options.text: It depends on whether you are exercising
options.feedback: Exercise changes how fast, not which way. Blood always arrives at the lungs with more carbon dioxide than the air in the alveolus.

items.stem: What happens to breathing during exercise?
items.skill: Give both changes the outcome names

options.text: Both the rate and the depth of breathing increase
options.feedback: Both, and both are named in the specification, so both are marking points.

options.text: Only the rate of breathing increases
options.feedback: Half the answer. Each breath also becomes deeper, taking in more air.

options.text: Only the depth of breathing increases
options.feedback: Also half. The number of breaths per minute goes up too.

options.text: The rate increases and the depth decreases
options.feedback: Both go up. More oxygen is needed and more carbon dioxide must be removed, so more air is moved in both ways.

items.stem: Two students are compared after exercise. Which sentence would earn the evidence mark?
items.skill: Quote data when giving evidence from a graph

options.text: Y is fitter because Y's resting rate is 12 breaths per minute and X's is 16
options.feedback: Both students named and both numbers quoted. That is what 'use evidence from the graph' means.

options.text: Y is fitter because Y breathes less
options.feedback: No numbers and no time period. March 2026 examiners asked for evidence from the graph, and this sentence could have been written without looking at it.

options.text: Y is fitter because Y did more exercise
options.feedback: Both students exercised for the same time — the graph shows that. Read it before concluding.

options.text: Y is fitter because fitness improves breathing
options.feedback: That restates the question. The mark is for what the graph shows.

parts.stem:
Which explanation goes with this adaptation of the alveolus?

The lining is moist.

options.feedback: A moist lining allows the gases to dissolve, because a gas has to be in solution before it can cross the wall.
A short distance comes from the wall being thin. The moist lining lets the gases dissolve first.
Surface area comes from there being many alveoli. The moist lining lets gases dissolve.
Maintaining the gradient is the blood supply's job — it carries gases away. The moist lining lets them dissolve.
Warmth is not one of the adaptations of a respiratory surface, and it is not what a moist lining does.

scheme.for: The lining is moist. — allows gases to dissolve

hints: Ask what has to happen to a gas before it can cross a wet surface.
parts.workedSolution: A moist lining allows the gases to dissolve, because a gas has to be in solution before it can cross the wall.

parts.stem:
Which explanation goes with this adaptation of the alveolus?

The wall is one cell thick.

options.feedback: Dissolving is what the moist lining does. A thin wall shortens the distance the dissolved gas then has to travel.
A thin wall gives a short diffusion distance, so gases cross quickly.
Surface area comes from there being many alveoli. A thin wall shortens the diffusion distance.
Maintaining the gradient is the blood supply's job. A thin wall shortens the distance.
Warmth is not one of the adaptations of a respiratory surface. A thin wall shortens the diffusion distance.

scheme.for: The wall is one cell thick. — gives a short diffusion distance

hints: Thin is about distance, not area.
parts.workedSolution: A thin wall gives a short diffusion distance, so gases cross quickly.

parts.stem:
Which explanation goes with this adaptation of the alveolus?

There are millions of alveoli.

options.feedback: Dissolving is what the moist lining does. Having many alveoli changes the area available, not whether gases dissolve.
A short distance comes from the wall being thin. Many alveoli give a large surface area instead.
Many alveoli give a large surface area, so more gas can cross at once.
Maintaining the gradient is the blood supply's job. Many alveoli give a large surface area.
Warmth is not one of the adaptations of a respiratory surface. Many alveoli give a large surface area.

scheme.for: There are millions of alveoli. — gives a large surface area

hints: Many small sacs add up to a very large total area.
parts.workedSolution: Many alveoli give a large surface area, so more gas can cross at once.

parts.stem:
Which explanation goes with this adaptation of the alveolus?

Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries.

options.feedback: Dissolving is what the moist lining does. The blood supply's job is to keep a difference in concentration across the wall.
A short distance comes from the wall being thin. A good blood supply maintains the difference in concentration.
Surface area comes from there being many alveoli. A good blood supply maintains the concentration difference.
A good blood supply carries gases away and brings more, so the diffusion gradient is maintained.
Warmth is not one of the adaptations of a respiratory surface. A good blood supply maintains the diffusion gradient.

scheme.for: Each alveolus is wrapped in capillaries. — maintains the diffusion gradient
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 B1 F Q3: only the better candidates linked all the adaptations to the correct explanations.

hints: Ask what would happen to the concentration difference if the blood stopped flowing.
parts.workedSolution: A good blood supply carries gases away and brings more, so the diffusion gradient is maintained.

context.setting: An alveolus drawn with a capillary and two blank arrows

figures.alt: One alveolus with a blood capillary beside it, and two unlabelled arrows showing gases crossing between them in opposite directions.

parts.stem: Name the gas that diffuses from the air in the alveolus into the blood.

scheme.for: oxygen

parts.stem: Explain why this gas diffuses in that direction.

accepted: there is a higher concentration of oxygen in the alveolus than in the blood, so it diffuses down the concentration gradient

scheme.for: the concentration of oxygen is higher in the alveolus than in the blood
so oxygen diffuses down the concentration gradient into the blood

hints: Say which side has more of it, then name the process.
parts.workedSolution: The air in the alveolus has a higher concentration of oxygen than the blood arriving from the body, so oxygen diffuses down the concentration gradient into the blood.

commonErrors.feedback: Gases cross a respiratory surface by diffusion, down a concentration gradient. No energy is used.

parts.stem: Explain how the blood supply keeps gas exchange going.

accepted: blood carries the oxygen away and brings more carbon dioxide, so the concentration difference is maintained

scheme.for: the blood carries the oxygen away from the alveolus and brings carbon dioxide to it
so the diffusion gradient (concentration difference) is maintained

hints: Two marks: what the blood does, and what that means for the gradient.
parts.workedSolution: The blood flowing past carries oxygen away as fast as it arrives and keeps delivering carbon dioxide, so the concentration difference across the wall never disappears and diffusion continues.

commonErrors.feedback: The blood's job is described but not its effect. The second marking point is the words 'maintains the diffusion gradient'.

parts.stem:
A frog exchanges some of its gases through its skin. The skin is thin, kept moist, and richly supplied with blood capillaries.
Suggest two reasons why the frog's skin works as a respiratory surface.

accepted: it is thin, giving a short diffusion distance, and it has a good blood supply that maintains the diffusion gradient

scheme.for: any two from: thin, so a short diffusion distance / moist, so gases dissolve / good blood supply, so the diffusion gradient is maintained — [1] each
scheme.examinerNote: The adaptation on its own is not enough; the reason carries the mark.

hints: The stem gives you three features. Pair each with what it does.
Naming the feature without its reason is half a point.
parts.workedSolution: The skin is thin, so gases have only a short distance to diffuse, and it is kept moist so gases dissolve before diffusing. Its rich blood supply carries gases away, maintaining the diffusion gradient.

commonErrors.feedback: The features have been copied from the stem without saying what each one does. The reason is where the mark is.

context.setting: A student running up a flight of stairs

parts.stem: State two ways in which breathing changes during exercise.

accepted: the rate of breathing increases and the depth of breathing increases

scheme.for: the rate of breathing increases
the depth of breathing increases

hints: The specification names exactly two changes.
parts.workedSolution: The rate of breathing increases and the depth of breathing increases.

commonErrors.feedback: Only the rate is there. Depth — how much air per breath — is the second named change and the second mark.

accepted: the muscles respire faster so they need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide, which must be removed

scheme.for: the muscles are respiring faster
so more oxygen must be taken in and more carbon dioxide removed

hints: Start with what the muscle cells are doing, then what they need.
parts.workedSolution: The muscles respire faster during exercise, so they need more oxygen delivered and produce more carbon dioxide that has to be removed. Breathing deeper and faster moves more air to do both.

commonErrors.feedback: Energy is released by respiration, not made. Write 'the muscles respire faster, releasing more energy'.

parts.stem:
Student X's breathing rate was 16 breaths per minute at rest and rose to 36 breaths per minute during exercise.
Calculate the percentage (%) increase in student X's breathing rate.
Show your working out.

parts.stem: Explain why student X's breathing rate stays above its resting value for several minutes after the exercise has stopped.

accepted: the muscles are still short of oxygen and carbon dioxide made during exercise still has to be removed

scheme.for: extra oxygen is still needed by the muscles

context.setting: A biology club comparing the lung of a mammal with the leaf of a plant

parts.stem:
Gas exchange happens across a respiratory surface in both animals and plants.
Describe the adaptations of a respiratory surface and explain how each one makes gas exchange faster.
Your written communication is assessed in this question, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; organised clearly; spelling, punctuation and grammar good enough that the meaning is clear throughout.
Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; organised with some clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: a large surface area, so more gas can cross at the same time
thin, often one cell thick, giving a short diffusion distance
moist, so the gases dissolve before they diffuse
permeable, so gases can pass through the surface
a good blood supply in an animal, carrying the gases to and from the surface
the diffusion gradient is maintained, so diffusion continues
an example in each kingdom: alveoli in a lung, spongy mesophyll and air spaces in a leaf

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted. Capital letters and full stops are part of the within-band judgement.

hints: Six adaptations, and each one needs a 'so that…'. A list with no reasons is capped low.
Name one example from an animal and one from a plant — the outcome says plants and animals.
parts.workedSolution: A respiratory surface has a large surface area, so a great deal of gas can cross at the same time. It is thin, usually one cell thick, which gives a short diffusion distance. It is moist, so gases dissolve before they diffuse across it, and it is permeable, so they can pass straight through. In an animal it has a good blood supply, which carries oxygen away and brings carbon dioxide, so the diffusion gradient is maintained and diffusion keeps going. In a mammal these features belong to the millions of alveoli in the lungs; in a plant, the spongy mesophyll and its air spaces do the same job.

commonErrors.feedback: This is a list of adaptations with no explanations. Each indicative point pairs a feature with what it does, so a bare list reaches Band C at best.

findTheMistake.stem:
Eve is asked: 'Student Y is fitter than student X. Give two pieces of evidence from the graph that support this. [2]'
Her answer:
studentWorking: Student Y is fitter because Y does not get as out of breath.
Student Y is fitter because Y is better at exercise.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Neither line uses the graph. 'Not as out of breath' is a description of how Y feels, not a reading, and the second line simply repeats the claim in the question. The graph offers three numbered comparisons and none of them has been taken.
correction: Student Y has a lower resting breathing rate: 12 breaths per minute against 16 for student X.
Student Y reaches a lower highest rate during exercise: 28 breaths per minute against 36 for student X.
findTheMistake.feedback: No marks here, and the biology was probably right in her head. Both marks are for evidence, and evidence on this paper means a value read off the graph with both students named. March 2026's report says it directly: use evidence from the graph in your interpretation and conclusions. A useful habit is to write the two numbers down first and build the sentence round them.

prompts.prompt: List the six adaptations of a respiratory surface.
prompts.answer: Large surface area, thin, moist, permeable, good blood supply, and the diffusion gradient maintained.

prompts.prompt: Thin means a short ____ ____ ; moist means gases can ____ ; a good blood supply maintains the ____ ____ .
At an alveolus, which way does oxygen diffuse and which way does carbon dioxide diffuse?
prompts.answer: Oxygen diffuses out of the alveolus into the blood; carbon dioxide diffuses out of the blood into the alveolus. Each gas moves from where it is more concentrated to where it is less.

prompts.prompt: What two things happen to breathing during exercise, and why?
prompts.answer: The rate and the depth of breathing both increase, because the muscles respire faster and so need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide to remove.

prompts.prompt: How do you give 'evidence from a graph' so it scores?
prompts.answer: Name both things being compared, quote a value for each, and say which is higher or lower. A sentence with no number is not evidence.
